speaker_role: independent counselor / essay editor (Kevin, co-founder of ElevatEd School; self-described professional college counselor)
commercial_incentive: Sells essay-editing services through ElevatEd's website and plugs it during the video.
key_insights: Cut cliche opening lines and keep only the distinctive concrete detail; a half-blank quiz or a sensory image is more useful than stated emotion.
Avoid the 'Eureka problem': a sudden worldview change from one event reads as unbelievable, so show the shift as gradual with small concrete steps.
Replace vague chores or duties with exact tasks and times; specifics like a named pupil or a concrete routine make claims credible and often use fewer words.
Repetition of the same realization (purpose, calling, material science) is a very common flaw; state a point once and put reflection in the conclusion.
Conclusions should add real insight rather than restate; he suggests a structure of what I used to believe, how that shifted, and what I now think.
Prefer more detail early and trim later; keep vivid verbs, cut dramatic filler, avoid quotes from famous people, and cut weak compliments from others.
He says essays scoring around 6-7 on his own rubric, not a perfect 10, have gotten students into top schools.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Kevin says repetition appears in roughly 90-95% of essays sent to him (informal estimate).
He rates the first essay about 6.75/10 on his own rubric and says students with just over 6 have been admitted to Ivy-level and top-20 schools.
He rates the baking essay about 8/10 and his own Common App essay about 8.
ElevatEd edit turnaround claimed as three business days.
notable_or_distinctive: Line-by-line live edits with named failure patterns (Eureka problem, repetition, telling vs showing) and a concrete reflective-conclusion template.
reliability_notes: Scores and admission claims come from the speaker's own rubric and anecdotes with no data; auto-captions garble some words and the video promotes paid editing.
